540.title: While the mind still works
540.hook: hurry, not only because death nears, but because understanding may fail first (Meditations 3.1)
540.howItsDone: Some readers take this entry as a push to stop postponing tasks that need clear thinking, such as important letters, plans and conversations with older relatives.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was a stranger's sojourn: life as a traveler's stay, and the question of what guides you. Your line was a traveler's stay.

Watching a grandparent slowly lose their memory can bring a particular kind of sadness. The hands are still there, the laugh, the way they hold a cup. But the person who could tell you the story, or say the thing you were waiting to hear, is harder and harder to reach. Book three opens with a short note in the manuscripts: at Carnuntum, a fortress on the Danube. Then Marcus looks straight at that possibility for himself. Today: while the mind still works.
screen: `THE BODY STILL HERE.` → `THE PERSON HARDER TO REACH.` → `WHILE THE MIND STILL WORKS.`

segments.voice: Each day, Marcus begins, life is spent, and less of it remains. We've heard that from him, and from Seneca. Then he adds something new. Even if a person lives longer, it isn't certain the mind will stay able to understand things, to think about what's human and what's divine. Breathing, eating, imagining, wanting: those may carry on. What can go first is the power to use ourselves well: to see our duties clearly, to sort out appearances, to think something through. So, he says, we must hurry. Not only because death comes closer every day, but because understanding may stop before life does. It matters how we hear that. This isn't a judgment on anyone whose mind has changed with age or illness. A person's worth doesn't leave with their memory, and the people who care for them know it. Marcus is talking to himself, about timing. If something needs a clear mind, don't assume the clear mind will always be there: the letter to your children, the hard conversation, the will, the forgiveness, the thing you keep saying you'll learn. Even the talks with the older people you love, while they can still tell you the story. The urgency isn't panic. It's the steady push this path keeps meeting: now, not someday. Marcus just adds one more reason. Not only while I live. While I can.

Then think of one thing that needs this clear mind, something you've been putting off: a letter, a decision, a question for an older relative. Picture yourself doing it, while you can.

541.title: Answer openly
541.hook: think only thoughts you could say out loud if suddenly asked (Meditations 3.4)
541.howItsDone: Some people practicing Stoicism use Marcus's test during the day, asking whether their current thought is one they could say out loud without embarrassment.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was while the mind still works. Your line was while I can: do what needs a clear mind now.

Penny for your thoughts. Someone says it across the table, and for a split second there's a small panic. The honest answer might be: I was replaying that argument and winning it this time. Or comparing my life to my cousin's. Or wondering what those two are whispering about. So we say, oh, nothing. Marcus turns that little moment into a test, not for what you say, but for what you think. Today: answer openly.

Book three's fourth entry starts with a warning. Don't waste what's left of your life thinking about other people, Marcus says, unless it's for some common good: what so-and-so is doing and why, what they're saying, what they're scheming. All of that pulls you away from watching your own ruling part. Last week he warned against prying into other people's souls. Here it's how much of our own quiet thinking drifts to them. Then the test. Get used to thinking only thoughts that, if someone suddenly asked what you're thinking right now, you could answer at once, openly: this, or that. Then it would be plain, he says, that everything in you is simple and kind, fit for someone who lives among others. No thought of pleasure or indulgence, no rivalry, no envy, no suspicion, nothing you'd blush to admit. It's a high bar. But notice his verb: get used to it. A habit, built slowly. A person like that, he says, is like a priest and servant of the gods, at home with the divine within, untouched by pleasure, unhurt by pain, wrestling in the noblest contest, not overthrown by any passion. Readers on different paths hear that differently; Marcus meant the spirit within he tended all through book two. The test itself fits anyone. Not a vow of perfect thoughts. Just a question to ask before a thought settles in: could I say it?

542.title: If you find anything better
542.hook: if you find anything better than justice, truth, self-control and courage, turn to it; if not, make room for nothing else (Meditations 3.6)
542.howItsDone: Readers of Marcus Aurelius often use the four virtues of Meditations 3.6 as an evening check: was I just, truthful, self-controlled and brave today?

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was answer openly. Your line was could I say it: think only what you could say out loud.

Most advice tells you what to want. Marcus Aurelius does something stranger: he issues a challenge, aimed at himself. Go ahead, he says. Search all of human life. If you find something better than these four things, turn to it with your whole soul and enjoy it. He isn't defending a position. He's daring himself to beat it. An emperor who could have anything, asking what's actually worth having. Today: if you find anything better.
screen: `A CHALLENGE, AIMED AT HIMSELF.` → `SEARCH ALL OF HUMAN LIFE.` → `IF YOU FIND ANYTHING BETTER.`

segments.voice: The four are justice, truth, self-control and courage. Readers of Plato will hear the old Greek list of four virtues, where wisdom usually stands. Marcus puts truth in that place, which tells you something about him: for a man surrounded by flatterers, truth was a daily discipline. Then the dare. If you find anything better than these, turn to it. He raises the stakes: if you find anything better than the guiding spirit inside you, the reason that governs your choices and keeps you honest, take that instead. And he answers himself. If nothing better turns up, and he expects nothing will, make room for nothing else. Next come the rivals that usually crowd in: praise from the crowd, power, wealth, the enjoyment of pleasures. He doesn't call them evil. His worry is subtler. Let one sit beside the four as an equal, even briefly, and it starts to take over without asking. A second loyalty quietly becomes the first. So, he writes, simply and freely choose the better, and hold on to it. Not a long calculation every morning, weighing virtue against convenience. One plain choice, then kept. And it gives any day four questions. Was I fair? Was I true? Did I hold back where I needed to? Did I do the hard thing? The dare stays open.

segments.voice: Walk back through your day so far, or yesterday if it's early, and find one moment for each of the four: being fair, being true, holding back, doing the uncomfortable thing. Don't grade too hard. Just notice which got the most room, and which got crowded out.
Self-control. One of the four goods in Marcus's dare, alongside justice, truth and courage: if you find anything better, turn to it. If not, give room to nothing else. Today's word.
Your line: nothing better. One plain choice, made simply, then kept. Day five hundred forty-two, done.

543.title: Never break faith
543.hook: value nothing that makes you break your word or lose self-respect (Meditations 3.7)
543.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius treat Meditations 3.7 as a household test: if a desire only works in hiding, behind walls and curtains, they count it as a loss.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was self-control, one of Marcus's four goods. Your line was nothing better.

Curtains can tell you something about a house. Some hang there for warmth, or for sleep. And sometimes a curtain is there for another reason: the purchase nobody mentioned, the deleted message, the plan someone would rather nobody saw. Marcus Aurelius used curtains as a test. In the seventh entry of his third book he lists what a person should never count as worth having, and he ends the list with walls and curtains. Today: never break faith.
screen: `CURTAINS ON A HOUSE.` → `WHAT NEEDS CURTAINS?` → `NEVER BREAK FAITH.`

segments.voice: Never value anything as good for you, Marcus writes, if it will one day force you to break your word or lose your self-respect. Notice the order. He doesn't start with what's forbidden; he starts with what we value. If a thing would cost you your word, it was never really a gain. The list goes on: nothing that makes you hate anyone, suspect anyone, curse anyone, play the hypocrite. Each is a small way of breaking faith, with another person or with yourself. It ends with anything you'd want that needs walls and curtains around it. A plain household test: if a desire only works in hiding, Marcus counts it a loss, however good it looks. It echoes the test from two days ago: think only what you could say out loud. Then he sketches the person who keeps faith. They put their own mind and its goodness first. They don't make a tragedy of things, don't groan, and need neither solitude nor a crowd. They neither chase life nor run from it. Breaking faith is rarely one big betrayal. It's usually small: the call you said you'd make, the favor you said you'd do, the time you said you'd be there. A word that holds in small things is easier to trust in large ones. That's what Marcus is protecting: not a reputation, but a self you can respect.

544.title: Honor the power of judgment
544.hook: revere your capacity to form opinions; it keeps you free (Meditations 3.9)
544.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius practice Meditations 3.9 by pausing between an event and their verdict about it, separating what they saw from what they added.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Marcus, and his rule: never value what costs your word. Your line was keep faith.

Count the opinions you've formed today. The coffee is weak. That driver is a jerk. My boss is annoyed with me. That person on the train looks unfriendly. They pile up before lunch, fast and unnoticed, and they feel like seeing, not like deciding. Marcus Aurelius had a name for the quiet machine that turns what happens into what we think about it. He didn't just tell himself to use it. He told himself to revere it. Today: honor the power of judgment.
screen: `OPINIONS BEFORE LUNCH.` → `THEY CAN FEEL LIKE SEEING.` → `HONOR THE POWER OF JUDGMENT.`

segments.voice: In the ninth entry of book three, Marcus tells himself to revere the faculty that forms opinions. The Greek word means supposing, taking a thing to be so. In the Stoic picture, before you act, before you feel, you've already judged. That judging is the hinge. This power, Marcus says, is what keeps your mind from holding any opinion that goes against nature and against what a reasoning creature is meant to be. If it's careless, everything downstream is careless: the anger, the fear, the reply you send. If it's careful, the rest has a chance. He lists three gifts from a well-kept judgment. Freedom from hasty conclusions. Friendliness toward other people. And following the gods, which for a Stoic meant living in step with the order of things. Notice the second. Marcus ties careful judgment to friendliness, and it isn't hard to see why: unkindness often rests on a quick verdict about someone we barely know. This is the Stoic thread we've followed since Epictetus: you can't control what happens, but you can control what you take it to mean. A prisoner, a slave, an emperor, each has this power. No one can form an opinion for you unless you let them. Between the event and your verdict there's a small gap. Revering judgment just means using it. Is that what I saw, or what I decided?

segments.voice: Pick one opinion you formed quickly today, about a person or a situation, and say it to yourself in a sentence. Then slow it down: what did you actually see or hear, what did you add, and is there another story that fits the same facts? Form one careful opinion in its place; it may be the same verdict, or softer, but this time you chose it.

545.title: Only now
545.hook: each lives only this moment; the rest is gone or unknown (Meditations 3.10)
545.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius return to Meditations 3.10 when worry or regret pulls at them, bringing their attention back to the present moment.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was Marcus, revering the power of judgment. Your line was judge carefully.

Where are you right now? Not your body. Your mind. Maybe it's replaying a conversation from Tuesday, or rehearsing one for Friday. The past rides along like a backpack, the future hangs ahead like a weather forecast, and the one place you actually stand gets barely a glance. Marcus Aurelius set all of that down in a few short lines. Today: only now.
screen: `WHERE IS YOUR MIND?` → `TUESDAY BEHIND, FRIDAY AHEAD.` → `ONLY NOW.`

segments.voice: The tenth entry of book three opens with a clearing-out: throw everything else away, Marcus tells himself, and hold on to these few things. Each of us, he says, lives only the present, this moment that can't be divided. Everything else is either already lived or uncertain. That's not a mood. It's a description. You can't live yesterday again, and you can't yet live tomorrow. In his terms, the only life anyone actually has is happening in this breath. Then he widens the lens. Short is the life each person lives. Small is the corner of the earth where they live it. Short, too, is the longest fame after death, passed along by people who will soon die themselves, who don't know even themselves, let alone someone long gone. He isn't trying to depress himself. He's pulling his attention back from where it wanders, the regrets and the legacy, to the one place it can do any good. If the past is finished and the future unknown, neither is where your choices happen. The present is small, but it's the only part of life you can steer. Other contemplative traditions have their own words for returning to this moment. For Marcus, it's plain arithmetic. As he put it back in book two, the present is the only thing anyone can lose, because it's the only thing anyone has.

546.title: Define it
546.hook: describe each thing plainly, stripped bare, as it is (Meditations 3.11)
546.howItsDone: Some readers of Marcus Aurelius practice Meditations 3.11 by writing a worry down in one plain sentence, naming what it is and what it asks of them, before deciding how to respond.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was only now. Your line was only this: the one moment anyone lives. Today a week closes.

A worry rarely arrives in plain words. It arrives as a cloud. Something about money. Something about that test result. Something about the way she said goodnight. It's big and blurry and fills the room. Now try writing it down in one flat sentence, the way a clerk would. Sometimes the cloud shrinks the moment it has edges. Marcus Aurelius used this trick on himself, and wrote down how it works. Today: define it.
screen: `A WORRY ARRIVES AS A CLOUD.` → `WRITE IT LIKE A CLERK.` → `DEFINE IT.`

segments.voice: Book three's eleventh entry calls this one more aid to add to the others. Always make a definition, or a description, Marcus writes, of whatever presents itself to your mind. See what it is in substance, stripped bare, whole, and tell yourself its name and the names of the parts it's made of. His point is that what upsets us is often less the thing than the coat we put on it. A late bill becomes I'm failing at life. A curt email becomes they're about to fire me. Defining strips the coat off. A late bill is a piece of paper asking for an amount by a date. That may still be a problem, but now it's one you can see. Then he asks of each thing: what is it, what is it made of, how long will it last, and what does it ask of me? Gentleness, courage, truth, faithfulness, simplicity? A defined thing points to a response. A cloud just points to dread. Nothing so enlarges the mind, he says, as being able to examine everything that happens methodically and truly. Look at what this week has built. While I can. Could I say it. Nothing better. Keep faith. Judge carefully. Only this. And now, as it is. Seven short lines, each small enough to say in one breath.
